claims.text: FakeOrderRepository implements IOrderRepository's four methods with a Dictionary<int, Order>; AddAsync assigns order.Id from a counter starting at 1; SaveChangesAsync returns Task.CompletedTask; Seed (not in the interface) stores an order as-is.
FakeNotifier implements INotifier; Send appends (orderId, subject) to a public List Sent and does nothing else.
OrderService.PlaceOrderAsync calls repository.AddAsync and SaveChangesAsync, then uses order.Id in notifier.Send.
OrderServiceTests' CancelOrderAsync test uses FakeOrderRepository.Seed to place an order before acting.
Task.FromResult returns an already-completed Task with the given result; Task.CompletedTask is an already-completed Task.

There are several kinds of test double; this course calls a working, simplified implementation a fake, while other sources, including the .NET docs, use "fake" more loosely (for a stub or a mock). The stunt-double comparison is an analogy.
If AddAsync did not set Id, two added orders would both have Id 0 and the second would overwrite the first in the dictionary, so ListByCustomerAsync would return one order.
EfOrderRepository's constructor takes the concrete DonHangDbContext.
A fake only needs the behaviour the class under test and the test rely on.
In the real system PostgreSQL assigns an order's id (identity column) when SaveChangesAsync inserts the row; EF Core copies it back to order.Id.
